title: BELA Act 2: Attendance, discipline and learner safety
description: Compulsory Grade R, monitoring attendance, the new penalties, code of conduct and suspension changes, and the bans on corporal punishment and initiation.

lessons.title: Compulsory Grade R and school attendance
lessons.summary: Who must be in school, from when, until when, and who is responsible for making it happen.
lessons.body:
## 🏫 The new rule in one sentence

Every parent must cause every learner they are responsible for to attend school, **starting from Grade R** on the first school day of the year in which the learner turns **six**, and not leaving school until the last school day of the year in which the learner turns **15** or will complete **Grade 9**, whichever comes first (SASA s3(1) as amended by BELA s2).

## 🔄 What changed

- **Before BELA:** compulsory school started in the year a child turned seven (normally Grade 1). Grade R was offered at many schools but parents did not have to send their child.
- **After BELA:** Grade R is part of compulsory schooling. SASA s1 now defines "grade R" as the Reception grade.
- The end point is also clearer: the year the learner turns 15 or will complete Grade 9, whichever happens first.

This has been law since the BELA Act commenced on 24 December 2024.

## 👨‍👩‍👧 Who carries the duty?

1. **Parents.** The duty in SASA s3(1) is on the parent. SASA uses "parent" broadly, so it can include a guardian or the person who has custody of the learner.
2. **The province.** Every MEC must make sure there are enough school places so that every child in the province can attend school as required (SASA s3(3)). If there is a lack of capacity, the MEC must fix it as soon as possible and report each year to the Minister (SASA s3(4)).
3. **The Minister** must set the ages of compulsory attendance for learners with special education needs by notice in the Gazette (SASA s3(2)).
4. **Schools.** Educators, principals and governing bodies must promote and monitor attendance (SASA s4A, inserted by BELA s3). Lesson 2 covers this.

## 🏡 Does "school" include independent schools and home education?

Yes to independent schools. SASA s1 defines a "school" as a public school or an independent school. A parent who enrols their child in a registered independent school's Grade R meets the duty in SASA s3(1).

Home education is the other lawful option. A learner who is **registered with the HOD** to receive home education is exempt from school attendance (SASA s51(7) as substituted by BELA s35). An unregistered home schooler is not exempt.

> 💡 Tip: A parent asks at the school gate: "My daughter turns six in November. Must she do Grade R this year?" Under SASA s3(1) the duty starts on the first school day of the year in which she turns six, so yes, she must attend Grade R in that year, at a public school, a registered independent school, or through registered home education.

## 🧱 Grade R capacity

Making Grade R compulsory means provinces need enough Grade R classes, practitioners and space. National and provincial departments have acknowledged that capacity differs between provinces and that the rollout is still being resourced.

> ⚠️ Watch out: The legal duty is already in force, but how your province is placing Grade R learners, and any admission dates for Grade R, depend on provincial circulars. Ask your district office for the current Grade R admission circular before you answer parents. Admission rules themselves are covered in BELA 3.

## 🗓️ A school example

At the January SGB meeting of a public primary school, the principal reports 30 Grade R applications for 25 places. The SGB cannot fix capacity on its own. The principal should report the shortfall to the district, because the MEC carries the duty to provide enough places (SASA s3(3)). Admission decisions follow the school's admission policy and SASA s5 (see BELA 3).

## ✅ Key points

- Compulsory schooling now starts at Grade R, in the year the child turns six (SASA s3(1), BELA s2).
- It ends in the year the learner turns 15 or will complete Grade 9, whichever comes first.
- Parents carry the duty; the MEC must provide enough places (SASA s3(3)).
- Registered home education exempts a learner from school attendance (SASA s51(7)).
- Check the current provincial Grade R circular with your district office.

lessons.title: Monitoring attendance and the penalties
lessons.summary: What the school must do when a learner is absent, and the offences for keeping a learner out of school or disrupting it.
lessons.body:
## 🚨 Schools now have a legal duty to watch attendance

BELA inserted a new section into SASA called "Monitoring learner attendance" (SASA s4A, inserted by BELA s3). It says:

1. The **educator, principal and governing body** are responsible for promoting and monitoring the attendance of learners at school (s4A(1)).
2. The governing body must make sure the **code of conduct for learners** contains rules on **punctuality and regular school attendance** (s4A(2)).
3. If a learner is absent for **three consecutive school days** without a valid reason, the **class teacher must report** the absence to the principal (s4A(3)).
4. The principal must, **within 24 hours** of being told, investigate by making a reasonable effort to contact the parent, by whatever means suit the school and the family, and report the matter to the **governing body** for further intervention (s4A(4)).

> 💡 Tip: Put a simple attendance step in your school routine: register taken daily, class teacher flags day three, principal phones or messages the parent the next day and logs it, and the SGB or board gets a short absence report at each meeting.

The code of conduct duty in s4A(2) applies to the code of conduct that a public school governing body must adopt under SASA s8. Independent schools should check with their association how they build these steps into their own rules.

## 🏛️ What the HOD can do

If a learner who must attend school is not enrolled or does not attend, the HOD may investigate, take appropriate measures to remedy the situation, and, failing that, issue a **written notice** to the parent requiring compliance (SASA s3(5)).

## ⚖️ The offences and penalties

SASA s3(6), as substituted by BELA s2(b), now reads in short:

- **Parents.** A parent who, **without just cause and after a written notice from the HOD**, fails to send the learner to school is guilty of an offence. The penalty is a fine or imprisonment for up to **12 months**, or both, or another sentence within the court's discretion under the Criminal Procedure Act (s3(6)(a)).
- **Anyone else.** Any other person who, **without just cause**, prevents a learner who is subject to compulsory attendance from attending school is guilty of an offence, with the same maximum of 12 months (s3(6)(b)).

Before BELA the maximum prison term in s3(6) was **six months**. BELA doubled it.

Notice the protections for parents: there must be no just cause, and there must first be a written notice from the HOD. The law aims to get the child back in school, not to rush to prosecution.

## 🚧 Disrupting school is now an offence

BELA added SASA s3(7): any person who **unlawfully and intentionally** interrupts, disturbs or hinders any official educational activity of a school, or hinders or obstructs a school in performing its official educational activities, is guilty of an offence. The penalty is a fine or imprisonment for up to 12 months, or both.

> ⚠️ Watch out: Examples where s3(7) may be relevant: a group blocking the school gate so learners cannot enter during a community protest, or someone forcing a school to send learners home. Whether a charge succeeds is for the police, prosecutor and court. The school's job is to keep learners safe, record what happened and report it to SAPS and the district.

## 👧 A school example

Thandi in Grade 4 has missed Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday with no message. On Wednesday afternoon her class teacher reports it to the principal (s4A(3)). On Thursday morning the principal phones and sends a message to her grandmother, who is her caregiver, and learns Thandi is looking after a sick sibling. The principal logs the contact and reports it to the governing body (s4A(4)), and the school links the family with support. No offence arises: the aim is to help Thandi back to school.

## ✅ Key points

- Educators, the principal and the governing body must promote and monitor attendance (SASA s4A(1)).
- Three consecutive unexplained days: teacher reports to the principal; the principal investigates within 24 hours and reports to the governing body (s4A(3) and (4)).
- A parent commits an offence only without just cause and after a written HOD notice; the maximum is now 12 months (s3(6)(a)).
- Preventing a learner from attending, or disrupting school activities, is an offence with up to 12 months (s3(6)(b) and s3(7)).

lessons.title: Code of conduct, discipline and suspension
lessons.summary: How BELA changed the code of conduct, exemptions, drugs and liquor rules, and suspension at public schools.
lessons.body:
## 📋 Who this lesson is for

SASA s8 and s9 deal with the code of conduct and suspension at **public schools**. If you serve on a board of governors at an independent school, your discipline rules come from your own constitution and contracts, but the constitutional principles of fairness still apply, and many independent schools follow similar steps.

## 🤝 The code of conduct: built with the school community

A governing body of a public school must adopt a code of conduct for learners **after consultation with learners, parents and educators** (SASA s8(1) as amended by BELA s7).

The code must aim at a disciplined and purposeful school environment and must now take into account the **diverse cultural beliefs, religious observances and medical circumstances** of learners at the school (SASA s8(2)).

## 🙋 The new exemption clause

Every learner must still follow the code of conduct (SASA s8(4)(a)). But the code **must contain an exemption provision** (SASA s8(4)(b)):

1. A learner, or the learner's parent, may apply to the governing body to be exempted from certain rules on grounds including, but not limited to, **cultural beliefs, religious observances and medical grounds**.
2. The governing body must give its decision **within 14 days** of receiving the application, and give **written reasons** if it refuses (s8(4)(c)).
3. If refused, the learner or parent may **appeal to the HOD within 14 days**. The HOD must decide within 14 days of receiving the appeal and give written reasons (s8(4)(d)).

> 💡 Tip: Example: a parent asks that her son may wear a religious head covering, or that a learner with a skin condition may wear a different school shoe. Have a simple application form, diarise the 14 days, and minute the SGB's decision and reasons.

## 🧒 Discipline must be age-appropriate

Disciplinary proceedings must be **age-appropriate**, conducted in the **best interests of the learner**, and follow the principles of natural justice, fairness and reasonableness (SASA s8(5)(c), added by BELA s7(d)). A Grade 2 learner and a Grade 11 learner should not be treated in the same way.

## 💊 Drugs and liquor

BELA changed SASA s8A so that it speaks of "a drug" or "any drug", not only "illegal" drugs (BELA s8). Unless the principal authorises it for legitimate educational purposes, no person may bring a dangerous object or a drug onto school premises or have it during a school activity (s8A(1)). A learner may face disciplinary proceedings if liquor, a dangerous object or any drug is found in their possession, or if their sample tests positive for liquor or any drug (s8A(12)).

## ⏸️ Suspension as a precaution

SASA s9(1), as substituted by BELA s9, now has two routes for a learner **accused** of serious misconduct:

- **Route (a): representations first.** For listed misconduct, such as assault with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, harassment including through social media, repeated bullying, illegal possession of a drug or liquor, repeated disruption of the school programme, serious exam transgressions, fraud, theft, possessing a dangerous object or pornographic material, and sexual activity or sexual assault at school, the governing body may suspend only **after giving the learner a reasonable opportunity to make representations**.
- **Route (b): immediate suspension.** Where the learner has been **formally charged by SAPS** with serious crimes such as murder, a sexual offence including rape, robbery, theft, or supplying drugs, committed on school premises or at a school activity, the governing body **must suspend immediately** without first hearing representations.

> ⚠️ Watch out: Suspension is a precaution, not the final outcome. Rules on the disciplinary hearing, timelines and expulsion are in the rest of SASA s9 and your provincial regulations. Check the current provincial rules with your district office before acting.

## ✅ Key points

- The code of conduct is adopted after consulting learners, parents and educators, and must respect diverse cultural, religious and medical circumstances (SASA s8(1) and (2)).
- It must contain an exemption clause: SGB decides in 14 days, appeal to the HOD in 14 days (s8(4)).
- Discipline must be age-appropriate and fair (s8(5)(c)).
- Suspension: representations first for most serious misconduct; immediate suspension if formally charged by SAPS with listed crimes (s9(1)).

lessons.title: Corporal punishment, initiation, home education and pregnancy
lessons.summary: The full ban on corporal punishment and initiation, plus what BELA does and does not say about home education and learner pregnancy.
lessons.body:
## 🛡️ Corporal punishment is abolished

Corporal punishment was already banned in South African schools. BELA makes the rule wider and clearer. SASA s10(1), as substituted by BELA s10, now says corporal punishment is **abolished** and no person may inflict or impose it on a learner:

- **at a school**,
- **during a school activity** (for example a sports tour or camp), or
- **in a hostel** accommodating learners of a school.

Because SASA defines "school" to include independent schools (SASA s1), this applies to **public and independent schools**.

### 📖 What counts as corporal punishment?

BELA added a definition to SASA s1. Corporal punishment means any deliberate act against a child that inflicts pain or physical discomfort, **however light**, to punish or contain the child. It includes, but is not limited to:

- hitting, smacking, slapping, pinching or scratching, with the hand or any object
- kicking, shaking, throwing, pulling hair, boxing ears, pulling or pushing
- forcing children to stay in uncomfortable positions, denying meals, forcing exercise that is not part of the curriculum, or denying or restricting toilet use
- any acts which seek to belittle, humiliate, threaten, induce fear or ridicule the dignity and person of a learner

> ⚠️ Watch out: The last item means corporal punishment is not only physical. A teacher who humiliates a learner in front of the class as punishment, or a hostel parent who sends boys out to do punishment push-ups at night, may fall within the definition.

### ⚖️ The penalty

Anyone who contravenes s10(1) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine or imprisonment, or both, as the court decides after considering the circumstances (SASA s10(2)). Before BELA it was punished with a sentence that could be imposed for assault.

## 🚫 Initiation practices

SASA s10A(1), as substituted by BELA s11, says no person may conduct or participate in any initiation practices against a learner at a school, **during a school activity** (new), or in a hostel.

- "Initiation practices" means any act done to initiate, admit or affiliate someone into, or keep their membership of, a school, group, activity, sports team or organisation, that, among other things, endangers mental or physical health or safety, treats some as inferior, subjects people to humiliating or violent acts, or destroys property (SASA s10A(3)).
- A person who contravenes s10A(1) is guilty of misconduct and disciplinary action must be instituted under the applicable code of conduct (s10A(2)(a)).
- The learner may also bring a civil claim against those who manipulated and forced them to take part (s10A(2)(b)).

> 💡 Tip: Brief Grade 8 and hostel leaders at the start of each year that "welcome week" traditions, tour rituals and team "initiations" are covered, including away from the school grounds during a school activity.

## 🏠 Home education: yes, BELA covers it

BELA substituted SASA s51 (BELA s35). In short: a parent who chooses home education must apply to the HOD to register the learner (s51(1)). If the HOD does not respond within 60 days, the application is deemed approved, as long as the parent can prove they applied (s51(6)). A registered learner is exempt from school attendance (s51(7)). A parent can appeal to the MEC within 30 days against a refusal or cancellation (s51(14)). For a school, the practical point is simple: if a parent withdraws a learner to home school, the learner must be registered, or the compulsory attendance duty in s3(1) still applies.

## 🤰 Learner pregnancy: only a regulation power

BELA does **not** set rules on how a school must handle a pregnant learner. It adds a power for the Minister to make regulations "on the management of learner pregnancy" (SASA s61(aA), inserted by BELA s39). Until such regulations are made, follow the national Department of Basic Education policy on learner pregnancy and your provincial circulars, and ask your district office for the current version.

## ✅ Key points

- Corporal punishment is abolished at school, during school activities and in hostels, at public and independent schools (SASA s10(1), BELA s10).
- The definition covers light physical punishment and acts that humiliate or belittle (SASA s1).
- Initiation practices are banned, now also during school activities; victims may sue (SASA s10A, BELA s11).
- Home education must be registered with the HOD (SASA s51, BELA s35).
- On pregnancy, BELA only lets the Minister make regulations (SASA s61(aA)).

questions.text: In which year must a child start Grade R under SASA s3(1) as amended by BELA s2?

options.text: The year the child turns five
The year the child turns seven
The year the child turns six
Whenever the parent chooses before Grade 1

questions.explanation: SASA s3(1), as amended by BELA s2, requires attendance from Grade R on the first school day of the year in which the learner reaches the age of six.

questions.text: Who must ensure there are enough school places for every child in the province?

options.text: The MEC for education in that province
The SGB or board of governors of each school
The principal of the nearest school
The parents' association

questions.explanation: SASA s3(3) places the duty to provide enough school places on every MEC, with s3(4) requiring capacity to be remedied and reported on annually.

questions.text: A learner has been absent for three consecutive school days with no valid reason. What must happen first?

options.text: The SGB must call a disciplinary hearing
The class teacher must report the absence to the principal
The school must open a case with SAPS
The HOD must fine the parent

questions.explanation: SASA s4A(3), inserted by BELA s3, requires the class teacher to report three consecutive days of absence without valid reason to the principal.

questions.text: Once the principal is told about the absence, what does SASA s4A(4) require?

options.text: Wait until the end of the term and include it in the report card
Suspend the learner for poor attendance
Within 24 hours, make a reasonable effort to contact the parent, investigate, and report to the governing body
Remove the learner from the register after five days

questions.explanation: SASA s4A(4), inserted by BELA s3, requires the principal to investigate within 24 hours by reasonable efforts to contact the parent, and report to the governing body.

questions.text: When can a parent be convicted for failing to send a learner to school under SASA s3(6)(a)?

options.text: Only without just cause and after a written notice from the HOD
Whenever the learner misses more than 10 days in a term
Only if the SGB lays a charge
Immediately after the first unexplained absence

questions.explanation: SASA s3(6)(a), as substituted by BELA s2(b), requires both the absence of just cause and a prior written notice from the HOD. The maximum prison term is now 12 months.

questions.text: What maximum prison term did BELA set for a person who prevents a learner from attending school without just cause?

options.text: Three months
Six months
Five years
12 months

questions.explanation: SASA s3(6)(b), as substituted by BELA s2(b), increased the maximum from six to 12 months, or a fine, or both.

questions.text: A parent applies for her daughter to be exempted from a uniform rule for religious reasons. What does the amended SASA s8(4) require of the SGB?

options.text: A decision within 30 days, with no need for reasons
Referral of the application straight to the HOD
A decision within 14 days, with written reasons if it refuses
Approval only if all other parents agree

questions.explanation: SASA s8(4)(c), as amended by BELA s7, requires the governing body to decide within 14 days and give written reasons for a refusal. An appeal lies to the HOD within 14 days (s8(4)(d)).

questions.text: Under SASA s9(1)(b) as substituted by BELA s9, when must the governing body suspend a learner immediately without hearing representations?

options.text: When the learner has been formally charged by SAPS with a listed serious crime committed at school or a school activity
When a teacher reports the learner for late coming three times
When the parent has not paid school fees
Whenever any learner is accused of bullying for the first time

questions.explanation: SASA s9(1)(b), as substituted by BELA s9, requires immediate suspension where the learner is formally charged by SAPS with listed offences such as murder, rape, robbery or drug supply at school or a school activity.

questions.text: A hostel parent makes a learner stand in an uncomfortable position for an hour as punishment. Under SASA as amended by BELA, this is:

options.text: Allowed, because hostels are not part of the school
Corporal punishment, which is banned at school, during school activities and in hostels
Allowed if the parents signed the hostel rules
Only a concern at public schools, not independent schools

questions.explanation: SASA s1 (definition added by BELA s1) includes forcing children to stay in uncomfortable positions. SASA s10(1), as substituted by BELA s10, bans corporal punishment in hostels, and "school" includes independent schools.

questions.text: What does the BELA Act say about learner pregnancy?

options.text: It requires pregnant learners to leave school for one year
It sets out a full procedure every school must follow
It requires the SGB to adopt a pregnancy policy within 30 days
It only gives the Minister power to make regulations on the management of learner pregnancy

questions.explanation: BELA s39 inserted SASA s61(aA), allowing the Minister to make regulations on the management of learner pregnancy. The Act itself sets no procedure.
